Markov Decision Processes

A Markov Decision Process (MDP) is the mathematical frame for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. It has five parts: a set of states S, a set of actions A, a reward function R, transition probabilities P, and a discount factor gamma.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a board game: your position is the state, your move is the action, points are rewards, and the dice decide where you land next. You care about winning eventually, not just this turn.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

At each step the agent observes state s, picks action a from its policy, receives reward R(s,a), and transitions to s' with probability P(s'|s,a). The goal is to maximize expected discounted return: the sum of gamma^t times reward at each future step t.

📝 KEY IDEA

The Markov property says the future depends only on the current state, not the full history. A well-designed state captures everything relevant, so the past can be forgotten.

A policy pi maps states to actions (or to a distribution over actions). The discount factor gamma (0 to 1) trades immediate versus future reward: near 0 is myopic, near 1 is far-sighted. For a robot navigating a grid, states are cells, actions are moves, reward is +1 at the goal and small negatives per step, so the optimal policy finds the shortest safe path.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Confusing reward with return. Reward is the immediate signal at one step; return is the discounted sum over the whole trajectory. RL optimizes return, not any single reward.

Q-Learning & Value Methods

Value-based methods estimate how good states or actions are, then act greedily. The action-value Q(s,a) is the expected return from taking action a in state s and behaving optimally thereafter.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a cheat sheet scoring every move in every situation. Once the scores are right, you just pick the highest-scoring move — no planning needed.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Q-learning updates toward a target: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + alpha[r + gamma*max Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]. The max over next actions makes it off-policy: it learns the optimal policy while possibly acting more randomly.

📝 KEY IDEA

The Bellman optimality equation ties a state's value to the best next value: Q*(s,a) = E[r + gamma*max Q*(s',a')]. Iterating this update converges to the optimum for tabular problems.

The key contrast is SARSA, an on-policy method that uses the action actually taken next: r + gamma*Q(s',a'). SARSA learns the value of the behavior policy (including its exploration), while Q-learning learns the greedy optimum. For a cliff-walking grid, SARSA takes a safer path, Q-learning learns the risky optimal edge.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Acting purely greedily too early. Without exploration (e.g. epsilon-greedy), the agent locks onto a suboptimal action before its Q-estimates are accurate.

Policy Gradients & Deep RL

Instead of learning values and acting greedily, policy-gradient methods parameterize the policy pi_theta directly and adjust theta to increase expected return. This handles continuous actions and stochastic policies naturally.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Rather than scoring every move and picking the best, you tune the dials of your instinct so that good outcomes become more likely and bad ones less likely.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

REINFORCE nudges the log-probability of each action up in proportion to the return that followed it: gradient = E[return * grad log pi_theta(a|s)]. Actions leading to high return get reinforced; low-return actions get suppressed.

📝 KEY IDEA

Subtracting a baseline (like a learned value V(s)) from the return lowers gradient variance without adding bias. This gives the advantage A = Q - V, the core of actor-critic methods.

In deep RL, neural nets approximate policies or values. DQN is value-based, using experience replay and a target network to stabilize Q-learning from pixels (e.g. Atari). PPO is a policy-gradient method that clips the update so the new policy stays close to the old, giving stable, reliable training — a common default today.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Expecting vanilla REINFORCE to be sample-efficient. Its gradients are high-variance, so it needs many episodes; baselines, advantages, and clipping (PPO) are what make deep RL practical.

Object Detection

Object detection finds where objects are and what they are, outputting a class label plus a bounding box for each object — unlike plain classification, which gives one label per image.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Classification says 'there is a dog'; detection draws a box around each dog and labels it, even when several share the frame.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

One-stage detectors like YOLO divide the image into a grid and predict boxes and class scores in a single pass, making them fast and real-time. Two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) first propose regions, then classify them, trading speed for accuracy.

📝 KEY IDEA

IoU = area of overlap / area of union between a predicted and ground-truth box. A prediction usually counts as correct when IoU exceeds a threshold like 0.5.

Because many overlapping boxes may fire on one object, non-max suppression (NMS) keeps the highest-confidence box and removes others with high IoU to it. Overall quality is summarized by mAP (mean Average Precision), averaging the precision-recall curve across classes and IoU thresholds. For a self-driving camera, a detector might output boxes for cars, pedestrians, and signs each frame.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Forgetting NMS. Without it a model reports dozens of duplicate boxes on the same object, inflating false positives and wrecking precision.

Image Segmentation

Segmentation labels images at the pixel level. Semantic segmentation assigns each pixel a class (road, sky, car) but does not separate individual objects. Instance segmentation distinguishes separate objects of the same class (car #1 vs car #2). Panoptic unifies both.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Semantic segmentation is coloring by category, like a paint-by-numbers where all cars share one color. Instance segmentation gives each individual car its own color.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

U-Net uses an encoder that downsamples to capture context and a decoder that upsamples to recover resolution. Skip connections copy fine-grained features from encoder to decoder, sharpening boundaries. It was designed for biomedical images and remains a workhorse.

📝 KEY IDEA

Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN by adding a branch that predicts a binary mask for each detected box, giving instance segmentation: detection plus per-object pixel masks.

A common metric is IoU (also called the Jaccard index) between predicted and true masks, averaged as mean IoU. For medical imaging, U-Net can outline a tumor pixel-by-pixel from an MRI scan, supporting diagnosis and treatment planning.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming semantic segmentation separates individual objects. It does not — two touching cars become one blob of the 'car' class unless instance segmentation is used.

Vision Transformers

The Vision Transformer (ViT) applies the transformer architecture — originally from NLP — to images by treating an image as a sequence of patches.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Cut the image into a grid of small tiles, flatten each tile into a 'word', and read the picture like a sentence, letting attention decide which tiles relate to which.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Each patch (e.g. 16x16 pixels) is linearly projected into a token embedding. Positional embeddings are added so the model knows where each patch sits. A special class token is prepended; after several self-attention layers, its final representation is used for classification.

📝 KEY IDEA

Self-attention lets every patch directly attend to every other patch, giving a global receptive field from the first layer — unlike CNNs, which build up context locally.

ViTs have weaker inductive bias than CNNs (no built-in locality or translation equivariance), so they typically need large datasets or strong pretraining to shine; with enough data they match or beat CNNs. A ViT can classify a photo by splitting it into 196 patches (a 14x14 grid) plus one class token.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Training a ViT from scratch on a small dataset. Without CNN-style inductive biases it overfits or underperforms; pretraining or heavy augmentation is usually essential.

Scientific ML & Physics-Informed Neural Networks

Scientific machine learning (SciML) blends data-driven models with known physical laws. A leading example is the physics-informed neural network (PINN), which trains a network to satisfy a differential equation, not just fit data points.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Instead of only memorizing measurements, the network is graded on whether its predictions obey the laws of physics — like a student who must show the equations balance, not just guess answers.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A PINN represents the solution u(x,t) as a neural network. Using automatic differentiation, it computes derivatives and forms the PDE residual — how far the network violates the equation. The loss combines this residual with boundary/initial-condition and any data terms.

📝 KEY IDEA

Encoding physics as a soft constraint lets PINNs learn from sparse or noisy data and even solve inverse problems (recovering unknown parameters) where pure data-driven models would fail.

For example, a PINN can approximate the solution to the heat equation using only boundary data by minimizing the residual across sampled points. However, PINNs can be hard to train (stiff or multi-scale problems, competing loss terms) and are often slower or less accurate than mature classical solvers on well-posed forward problems.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming PINNs always beat traditional numerical methods. For standard forward PDEs, finite-element and finite-difference solvers are usually faster and more reliable; PINNs shine on inverse or data-scarce problems.

AI for Discovery (drug, climate, energy)

AI is accelerating scientific discovery across domains by learning patterns from data and screening vast possibility spaces far faster than experiment alone.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Instead of testing millions of candidates one by one in a lab, AI narrows the search to the most promising few — like a metal detector guiding where to dig.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

In drug discovery, models such as AlphaFold predict 3D protein structures from amino-acid sequences, and generative models design candidate molecules that bind a target. AI also predicts toxicity and binding affinity to prioritize which compounds to synthesize.

📝 KEY IDEA

Across science, AI acts as a surrogate or emulator: a fast learned approximation of an expensive simulation, enabling rapid screening and forecasting that would otherwise be computationally infeasible.

In climate, ML emulators speed up weather and climate forecasting and downscale coarse models to local resolution. In energy, AI optimizes power-grid dispatch, forecasts renewable output, discovers new battery and catalyst materials, and helps control fusion plasma. For instance, learned models have controlled tokamak magnetic fields in real time.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Treating an AI prediction as final truth. Structure predictions, candidate drugs, and forecasts still require experimental validation and physical verification before being trusted.

RL Theory & Computation Reference

⚙️ FORMULAS

Bellman expectation (policy π): V^π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,a)[R + γV^π(s')]. Bellman optimality: V*(s) = max_a Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,a)[R + γV*(s')] and Q*(s,a)=Σ_{s'}P[R+γ max_{a'}Q*(s',a')].

Q-learning: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)]. TD(0): V(s) ← V(s)+α[r+γV(s')−V(s)].

Policy gradient: ∇J = E[Σ_t ∇log π_θ(a_t|s_t) · A(s_t,a_t)]; REINFORCE uses return G_t as the estimator.

💡 KEY RESULTS

The Bellman optimality operator T is a γ-contraction in sup-norm: ‖TU−TV‖_∞ ≤ γ‖U−V‖_∞. By Banach fixed-point, value iteration converges geometrically to the unique V*, with error bound ‖V_k−V*‖_∞ ≤ γ^k‖V_0−V*‖_∞. An infinite stream of reward r discounted by γ sums to r/(1−γ); the effective horizon is 1/(1−γ).

📝 TECHNIQUE

For a small MDP, evaluate a fixed policy by solving the linear system (I−γP^π)V = R^π, or iterate backward on a finite/terminal chain. Baselines b(s) that do not depend on the action leave the policy-gradient unbiased while reducing variance; the advantage A=Q−V is the optimal such baseline choice.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Q-learning is off-policy: its target uses max over next actions regardless of the behavior policy, so it learns Q* while exploring. SARSA is on-policy (uses the actually-taken a'). TD(λ) interpolates between TD(0) (λ=0, low variance/high bias) and Monte Carlo (λ=1, unbiased/high variance).

Computer Vision Arithmetic Reference

⚙️ FORMULAS

Conv output size: O = ⌊(W + 2P − D(K−1) − 1)/S⌋ + 1 where D=dilation. Params of a conv layer (with bias): (C_in·K·K + 1)·C_out. MACs: H_out·W_out·C_out·C_in·K·K; FLOPs ≈ 2·MACs.

Receptive field (stride-aware): r_l = r_{l−1} + (K_l−1)·jump_{l−1}, jump_l = jump_{l−1}·S_l. For L stride-1 layers of kernel K: RF = 1 + L(K−1).

IoU = area(∩)/area(∪). Precision=TP/(TP+FP), Recall=TP/(TP+FN).

💡 KEY RESULTS

'Same' padding with stride 1 needs P=(K−1)/2·D. A ViT on a 224×224 image with 16×16 patches produces (224/16)²=196 patch tokens (197 with the [CLS] token); each patch is flattened to 16·16·3=768 values. Self-attention cost is O(N²·d) — doubling the token count quadruples attention compute.

📝 TECHNIQUE

Average Precision (AP) is the area under the precision–recall curve. VOC2007 uses 11-point interpolation; VOC2010+/COCO use the all-point (interpolated-envelope) area. mAP averages AP across classes (and IoU thresholds for COCO).

⚠️ SUBTLETY

NMS greedily keeps the highest-score box and removes overlapping boxes with IoU above a threshold; too-high a threshold keeps duplicate detections, too-low suppresses true nearby objects. Dilation enlarges the effective kernel to D(K−1)+1 without adding parameters.

📊 FIGURE — two calculations
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The padding, and the 16× blow-up

Dilated padding. Dilation inserts gaps between kernel taps, stretching the effective kernel to D(K−1)+1 = 2(3−1)+1 = 5. To keep the spatial size with stride 1 you need P = D(K−1)/2 = 2·2/2 = 2. Check with the output formula:

(W + 2P − D(K−1) − 1)/S + 1 = (W + 4 − 4 − 1)/1 + 1 = W ✓

Attention scaling. With 16×16 patches, a 224×224 image gives (224/16)² = 14² = 196 tokens, and 448×448 gives (448/16)² = 28² = 784 tokens — a 4× increase in N.

Attention is O(N²·d), so the compute grows by 4² = 16×. Doubling the image resolution quadruples the tokens and multiplies attention cost by sixteen, which is why high-resolution vision transformers need windowed or sparse attention.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Two formulas to keep. Dilation stretches the kernel to D(K−1)+1, so "same" padding at stride 1 is P = D(K−1)/2 — here 2. And since attention is quadratic in the token count, doubling the input resolution quadruples N and raises attention cost by 16×.

Scientific ML Rigor Reference

⚙️ FORMULAS

A PINN minimizes L = L_data + λ·L_phys, where the physics residual for a PDE N[u]=0 is L_phys = (1/N_c)Σ_i ‖N[u_θ](x_i,t_i)‖² evaluated at collocation points. Example (1D heat): residual r = u_t − α u_xx; (Burgers): r = u_t + u u_x − ν u_xx.

Derivatives u_t, u_x, u_xx come from automatic differentiation of the network output w.r.t. its inputs, not finite differences.

💡 KEY RESULTS

Reverse-mode AD gives the gradient of a scalar w.r.t. all inputs in one backward pass; obtaining a second-order term like u_xx requires differentiating through the first derivative graph (nested/second-order AD). AD is exact to machine precision — no truncation error, unlike finite differences whose error trades off with round-off.

📝 TECHNIQUE

Physics constraints are added as soft penalty terms (weighted residuals) rather than hard constraints because collocation-point PDE residuals cannot be enforced exactly by an unconstrained optimizer; the weight λ balances data fit against physics and controls training stiffness. Conservation laws can be built in via the residual (e.g., divergence-form fluxes) or hard-encoded architectures.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

An ill-conditioned problem (large condition number κ) amplifies input/round-off error by ≈κ: relative output error ≈ κ·(relative input error). Stiff PDEs and imbalanced loss terms cause gradient pathologies; loss re-weighting, normalization, and adaptive collocation improve conditioning and stability.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
